    38	
    39	To access the package contents, use one of the two following `import`

    41	
    42	```python
    43	import larpix.larpix as larpix  # use the larpix namespace
    44	# or ...
    45	from larpix.larpix import *  # import all larpix classes into the current namespace
    46	```
    47	
    48	### Endian-ness
    49	
    50	We use the convention that the LSB is sent out first and read in first.
    51	The location of the LSB in arrays and lists changes from object to
    52	object based on the conventions of the other packages we interact with.
    53	
    54	In particular, pyserial sends out index 0 first, so for `bytes` objects,
    55	index 0 will generally have the LSB. On the other hand, bitstrings
    56	treats the _last_ index as the LSB, which is also how numbers are
    57	usually displayed on screen, e.g. `0100` in binary means 4 not 2. So for
    58	`BitArray` and `Bits` objects, the LSB will generally be last.
    59	
    60	Note that this combination leads to the slightly awkward convention that
    61	the least significant bit of a bytestring is the *last bit* of the
    62	*first byte*. For example, if bits[15:0] of a packet are
    63	`0000 0010 0000 0001` ( = 0x0201 = 513), then the bytes will be sent out as
    64	`b'\x01\x02'`.
    65	
    66	### Creating a LArPix Chip
    67	
    68	The `Chip` object represents a single LArPix chip and knows about
    69	everything happening on the chip regarding configuration, data sent in,
    70	and data read out. To create a Chip, just provide the chip ID number
    71	(hard-wired into the PCB) and the index for the IO Chain (daisy chain)
    72	that the chip is part of:
    73	
    74	```python
    75	myChip = Chip(100, 0)
    76	```
    77	
    78	The Chip object uses these ID values when it creates data packets to
    79	ensure that the packet reaches the correct chip. And other objects use
    80	the ID values to ensure that received data from the physical chip makes
    81	its way to the right Chip object.
    82	
    83	The chip's configuration register is represented by the `myChip.config`
    84	attribute, which is an instance of the `Configuration` object.
    85	
    86	### The Configuration object
    87	
    88	The `Configuration` object represents all of the options in the LArPix
    89	configuration register. Each row in the configuration table in the LArPix datasheet
    90	has a corresponding attribute in the `Configuration` object. Per-channel
    91	attributes are stored in a list, and all other attributes are stored as
    92	a simple integer. (This includes everything from single bits to values
    93	such as "reset cycles," which spans 3 bytes.) **Warning**: there is
    94	currently no type checking or range checking on these values. Using
    95	values outside the expected range will lead to undefined behavior,
    96	including the possibility that Python will crash _or_ that LArPix will
    97	be sent bad commands.
    98	
    99	`Configuration` objects also have some helper methods for enabling and
   100	disabling per-channel settings (such as `csa_testpulse_enable` or
   101	`channel_mask`). The relevant methods are listed here and should be
   102	prefixed with either `enable_` or `disable_`:
   103	
   104	 - `channels` enables/disables the `channel_mask` register
   105	 - `external_trigger` enables/disables the `external_trigger_mask`
   106	    register
   107	 - `testpulse` enables/disables the `csa_testpulse_enable` register
   108	 - `analog_monitor` enables/disables the `csa_monitor_select` register
   109	
   110	Most of these methods accept an optional list of channels to enable or
   111	disable (and with no list specified acts on all channels). The exception
   112	is `enable_analog_monitor` (and its `disable` counterpart): the `enable`
   113	method requires a particular channel to be specified, and the `disable`
   114	method does not require any argument at all. This is because at most one
   115	channel is allowed to have the analog monitor enabled.
   116	
   117	The machinery of the `Configuration` object ensures that each value is
   118	converted to the appropriate set of bits when it comes time to send
   119	actual commands to the physical chip. Although this is not transparent
   120	to you as a user of this library, you might want to know that two sets of
   121	configuration options are always sent together in the same configuration
   122	packet:
   123	
   124	 - `csa_gain`, `csa_bypass`, and `internal_bypass` are combined into a
   125	   single byte, so even though they have their own attributes, they must
   126	   be written to the physical chip together
   127	
   128	 - `test_mode`, `cross_trigger_mode`, `periodic_reset`, and
   129	   `fifo_diagnostic` work the same way
   130	
   131	Similarly, all of the per-channel options (except for the pixel trim
   132	thresholds) are sent in 4 groups of 8 channels.
   133	
   134	Configurations can be loaded by importing `larpix.configs` and running
   135	the `load` function. This function searches for a configuration with the
   136	given filename relative to the current directory before searching the
   137	"system" location (secretly it's in the larpix/configs/ folder). This is
   138	similar to `#include "header.h"` behavior in C.
   139	
   140	Configurations can be saved by calling `chip.config.write` with the
   141	desired filename.
   142	
   143	Once the Chip object has been configured, the configuration must be sent
   144	to the physical chip. This is accomplished with the `Controller` object,
   145	which we'll discuss next.
   146	
   147	### Communicating with the physical LArPix chip
   148	
   149	Communication between the computer and the physical LArPix chip is
   150	handled by the `Controller` object and uses a Serial interface. (The
   151	interface specification is given in the fpga\_interface.txt file. It's
   152	based on RS-232 8N1.) To initialize a Controller object, simply provide
   153	the port you'd like to communicate over. For the envisioned normal
   154	application (with an FTDI chip as USB-serial bridge), this will likely
   155	be something like `/dev/ttyUSB0`.
   156	
   157	```python
   158	controller = Controller('/dev/ttyUSB0')
   159	```
   160	
   161	An important attribute of the Controller object is `chips`, which is a
   162	list of Chip objects controlled by the particular Controller. Add a
   163	single Chip object to the list with `controller.chips.append(myChip)`,
   164	or add a whole list with `controller.chips.extend(list_of_chips)`.

   167	attributes at some point, but their defaults should work in most cases:
   168	
   169	 - `baudrate`: default = 1000000 baud. Controls the number of bits per
   170	   second, including RS-232 start and stop bits.
   171	 - `timeout`: default = 1 second. Controls how long to wait before
   172	   ending a read command
